answer.evidence: Rows 0-4 are a light stone tread with a highlight on rows 0-1, followed by dark shadow on rows 5-7 that reads as a riser or eave. Row 8 is a light edge line starting a second tread, with a gray vertical face on rows 9-14. The brown dirt flanks on the left and right are flat vertical cliff sides, not receding side faces. Rows 15-31 are cobble ground that begins under a dark line on row 15. The tile reads as stairs cut into a south-facing cliff, with tread surfaces and front faces both visible.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts favour the candidate: 12 visible tones per tile against 7 for paving and 3 for grass, and 0% near-flat coverage. By eye it is weaker. The stairs read as a few horizontal bands of grey stone, each with a light tread edge and a darker riser, so only about 4 lightness steps. The references have 5-6 steps, and the paving has individually shaded cobbles. The candidate has no per-stone grain or speckle, so the bands look smooth and clean. The brown side posts and green cap are simple blocks with little internal variation. About 41% of the dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outline is partly tinted and partly neutral dark grey, which I call mixed. It is also a tiny, simple piece and is not as dense in craft detail as the Beodeul paving next to it. When in doubt, fail.
